title: Python Collections
description: Choose and operate on lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets using their real trade-offs.
learning_objectives: Select a collection from access and uniqueness needs

sections.title: Core mental model
sections.learning_objective: Select a collection from access and uniqueness needs
sections.markdown: A `list` is an ordered mutable sequence; use indexing and slicing when position matters. A `tuple` is an ordered immutable sequence useful for fixed records and hashable composite keys. A `dict` maps unique hashable keys to values and preserves insertion order. A `set` stores unique hashable members and is built for membership and set algebra.

examples.code:
skills = ['sql', 'python', 'sql']
unique = set(skills)
profile = {'name': 'Mina', 'skills': unique}
print(profile['name'], sorted(profile['skills']))

sections.title: Operations and trade-offs
sections.learning_objective: Use indexing, slicing, membership, mutation, and iteration
sections.markdown: Lists and tuples support zero-based indexing, negative indexing, and half-open slices such as `items[1:4]`. Dictionaries iterate over keys by default; use `.items()` for key-value pairs. Membership is normally linear for a list but average O(1) for dictionaries and sets. Mutation methods such as `append`, `update`, and `add` modify an object in place and often return `None`. These selection trade-offs should follow the data invariant, not habit.

sections.title: Worked practice
sections.learning_objective: Trace the concept on concrete data.
sections.markdown: Work from the input and state the invariant before coding. Choose by invariant, not habit: list for ordered changing data, tuple for a fixed record, dictionary for keyed lookup, and set for uniqueness or fast membership. A common bug is shallow aliasing: `backup = items` creates a second reference, not a copy. Other mistakes include indexing a set, assuming all dictionary keys exist, and modifying a collection while iterating over it. For an interview, narrate the observation, the rule you are applying, and the resulting value. That sequence makes reasoning inspectable and exposes hidden assumptions.
